text.p: These are leading stories in this morning's Paris newspapers.
-- French car market expected to lose momentum of 1996 when government incentive schemes boosted demand. French carmakers saw their market shares eroded last year.

-- Cabinet meeting to unveil two new members of the Bank of France Monetary Policy Council this morning as mandates of Jean Boissonnat and Bruno de Maulde expire. Markets do not expect dramatic change in French monetary policy.
-- Airbus consortium members meet today to discuss planned shift to limited company status.
-- European markets nervous as Wall Street plunges on fears of economic over-heating.

-- Forecast 2.5 percent growth for 1997 may not be strong enough to cut unemployment in France and in Germany, economists worry. Exports are expected to boost economies but are not seen as job-creating.
-- U.S.-based Morton International buys salt producers Salins du Midi and Salins de l'Est from Suez, considers further acquisitions.
-- Government incentive schemes boosted car sales in 1996, which rose by 10.5 percent over 1995 levels.
-- Tighter rules and controls to apply to retail sales periods in France. Winter sales season opened yesterday in France, today in Paris.
-- Betting at horse races picked up in 1996 after having lost ground for four years.

-- The newspaper expects president Jacques Chirac to name employers' federation vice president Pierre Guillen and former Credit Foncier governor Jean-Rene Bernard to the Bank of France monetary policy council.
The newspaper says new members may be in a position to weigh on monetary policy and possibly alter Jean-Claude Trichet's commitment to a strong currency, in favour of rate cuts.

-- Franco-German strains over European currency union likely to intensify in 1997 as Germans stress need for fiscal discipline and sound money, and French insist that politicians need leeway to ease policy to respond to economic pressures.
